It is becoming f*cking dangerous: Claude Opus 5.5. It turned a single image into a robot gorilla that can be taken apart literally down to the last screw

I just asked it to make a model and went to grab some coffee. When I returned, the result shocked me

How it works:

> The image set the general style, while every plate, joint, and hinge is pure three.js code
> Opus generated a single frame next to the original and spent 4 loops fixing flaws before moving on to the animation
> The first version looked too toy-like, so it went back to work and packed 187 joints and 311 parts into a powerful body and 4 limbs
> Each part is rendered in a single draw call and positioned on every frame through a chain of bends
> Every 1 to 2 seconds something triggers: latches unfasten, the chest plate flips open, and the inner unit extends and rotates
> At 0:16 the entire structure flies apart into its components during a 330 degree rotation and reassembles before the rotation finishes

25 seconds, 3,126 lines of code, and one gorilla that leaves on its own at the end

Only a few hundred people know about this skill, but I will share it with you

Leaving the link below

i can't comprehend why people run claude code on default settings

one settings change and every model gets its own job:

→ opus plans every task and advises when stuck
→ sonnet 5.5 writes the actual code
→ haiku handles every file search
→ a critic agent tries to break your diff before you merge

Opus thinks. The cheap models grind.

paste this into claude code 👇

Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json. Keep every hook, permission and plugin I already have. Then create the two agent files below and show me the diff.

```json
{
  "model": "opusplan",
  "advisorModel": "opus",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "modelSettings": {
    "claude-opus-5-5": { "effortLevel": "high" },
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": { "effortLevel": "medium" }
  },
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "haiku"
  }
}
```

~/.claude/agents/scout.md
```
---
name: scout
description: finds code fast. returns file paths and line numbers only.
model: haiku
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
```

```

name: critic
description: reviews a diff or plan before any task is called done
model: opus
tools: Read, Grep, Bash
---

```

virals.text:
GPU Engineering from Scratch 🚀

Found this excellent free, open-source learning resource that explains GPU architecture and performance engineering from the ground up.

It's called Before GPU Engineering, a structured digital notebook with 56 chapters listed across four phases.

What makes it useful is the approach: instead of jumping straight into CUDA or Triton, it builds an understanding of how GPUs actually execute programs, move data, and handle parallel workloads.

What's inside:
→ CPU vs GPU architecture and parallel computing
→ Warps, SIMT, threads, and thread blocks
→ Registers, shared memory, caches, and HBM
→ Compute-bound vs memory-bound workloads
→ Kernel launches, synchronization, and race conditions
→ Memory coalescing and access patterns
→ Occupancy, latency hiding, and register spilling
→ Arithmetic intensity and memory bottlenecks
→ Tiling, matrix multiplication, and GPU performance
→ Profiling and identifying kernel bottlenecks

The explanations connect hardware concepts to problems encountered in AI workloads, including attention and efficient matrix operations.

It's primarily a reading resource rather than a hands-on programming course, and some later chapters are still being written.

Perfect for AI/ML engineers and software developers who want to understand the hardware behind LLM training and inference before diving deeper into CUDA, Triton, and GPU kernel optimization.

Completely free.

outsiders.name: Tech with Mak
outsiders.text:
GPU Engineering from Scratch 🚀

Found this excellent free, open-source learning resource that explains GPU architecture and performance engineering from the ground up.

It's called Before GPU Engineering, a structured digital notebook with 56 chapters listed across four phases.

What makes it useful is the approach: instead of jumping straight into CUDA or Triton, it builds an understanding of how GPUs actually execute programs, move data, and handle parallel workloads.

What's inside:
→ CPU vs GPU architecture and parallel computing
→ Warps, SIMT, threads, and thread blocks
→ Registers, shared memory, caches, and HBM
→ Compute-bound vs memory-bound workloads
→ Kernel launches, synchronization, and race conditions
→ Memory coalescing and access patterns
→ Occupancy, latency hiding, and register spilling
→ Arithmetic intensity and memory bottlenecks
→ Tiling, matrix multiplication, and GPU performance
→ Profiling and identifying kernel bottlenecks

The explanations connect hardware concepts to problems encountered in AI workloads, including attention and efficient matrix operations.

It's primarily a reading resource rather than a hands-on programming course, and some later chapters are still being written.

Perfect for AI/ML engineers and software developers who want to understand the hardware behind LLM training and inference before diving deeper into CUDA, Triton, and GPU kernel optimization.

Completely free.
